citation: Two sources. (1) Stack Overflow, '2025 Developer Survey', AI section, https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/ai (methodology at https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/methodology), with the launch post: Erin Yepis, 'Developers remain willing but reluctant to use AI: The 2025 Developer Survey results are here', Stack Overflow Blog, URL dated 2025/07/29, https://stackoverflow.blog/2025/07/29/developers-remain-willing-but-reluctant-to-use-ai-the-2025-developer-survey-results-are-here/ (the live page now shows 'December 29, 2025' because it was re-published as a top-ten post of the year). (2) DORA (Google Cloud), 'State of AI-assisted Software Development 2025', report version v. 2025.2, PDF at https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/2025_state_of_ai_assisted_software_development.pdf, landing page https://dora.dev/dora-report-2025/. AI adoption chapter by Kevin M. Storer, Ph.D.
evidence_tier: Stack Overflow: vendor survey (large, self-selected, recruited through Stack Overflow's own channels). DORA: industry research report by a Google Cloud team with sponsors; survey plus interviews, Bayesian statistical modelling, not peer-reviewed.
access_status: Fully read for the passages cited. Stack Overflow AI results page, methodology page and blog post opened and the raw HTML text checked. DORA PDF downloaded and text-extracted; executive summary, key findings, trust section (pp. 30-31), friction section (p. 39), AI Capabilities Model intro (p. 50) and version control section (pp. 55-56) read directly.
sponsor_and_incentive: Stack Overflow sells Stack Internal ('the knowledge intelligence layer that powers enterprise AI') and data licensing to AI model builders; low trust in AI and a continued need for 'human-verified knowledge' supports its positioning, and the blog says the data 'validates our vision'. DORA is run by Google Cloud, which sells AI coding tools (Gemini) and cloud platforms; the report lists platinum and gold sponsors (logos only, not text-extractable). Its 'AI is an amplifier' framing and emphasis on platform engineering both fit a vendor that sells AI and platforms.

Experienced developers are the most cautious, with the lowest \"highly trust\" rate (2.6%) and the highest \"highly distrust\" rate (20%), indicating a widespread need for human verification for those in roles with accountability."
Stack Overflow AI results page, question wording: "How much do you trust the accuracy of the output from AI tools as part of your development workflow?"
Stack Overflow AI results page, complex tasks: "Complex tasks carry too much risk to spend extra time proving out the efficacy of AI tools."
Stack Overflow blog (Yepis): "In fact, trust in the accuracy of AI has fallen from 40% in previous years to just 29% this year."

Stack Overflow blog (Yepis): "The number-one frustration, cited by 45% of respondents, is dealing with \"AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite,\" which often makes debugging more time-consuming. In fact, 66% of developers say they are spending more time fixing \"almost-right\" AI-generated code." (Note: this swaps the two figures relative to the results page.)

DORA 2025, Executive summary, p. 3, 'Key takeaway: AI is an amplifier': "The research reveals a critical truth: AI's primary role in software development is that of an amplifier. It magnifies the strengths of high-performing organizations and the dysfunctions of struggling ones."
DORA 2025, Executive summary, p. 3: "Without this foundation, AI creates localized pockets of productivity that are often lost to downstream chaos."
DORA 2025, Key findings, p. 4: "Yet a notable portion (30%) currently report little to no trust in the code generated by AI, indicating a need for critical validation skills."

DORA 2025, Analysis and advice for technology leaders, p. 5: "This \"trust but verify\" approach is a sign of mature adoption. The conversation must shift from adoption to effective use. Your training programs should focus on teaching teams how to critically guide, evaluate, and validate AI-generated work, rather than simply encouraging usage."

DORA 2025, Key findings, p. 4: "Our new DORA AI Capabilities Model identifies seven foundational practices—including a clear AI policy, a healthy data ecosystem, and a user-centric focus—that are proven to amplify the positive impact of AI on organizational performance." (em dashes are the report's own)

DORA 2025, AI Capabilities Model, p. 50, the seven capabilities: "Clear and communicated AI stance", "Healthy data ecosystems", "AI-accessible internal data", "Strong version control practices", "Working in small batches", "User-centric focus", "Quality internal platforms".

DORA 2025, p. 50: "Of these, a set of seven AI capabilities showed substantial evidence of an interaction with AI use. That is, when teams paired these capabilities with AI adoption, the difference AI made across important outcomes was amplified."

DORA 2025, Trust, p. 30: "Our findings suggest that absolute trust is not a prerequisite for AI-generated outputs to be useful. This pattern aligns with established behaviors; during our interviews, developers compared this to the healthy skepticism they apply to other widely-used resources, such as solutions found on Stack Overflow, where information is used, but not always implicitly trusted."

DORA 2025, Friction, p. 39: "For an individual, friction doesn't vanish so much as move: It shifts from manual grind to deciding and verifying, possibly in the form of prompt iteration, result vetting, and assessing code that looks remarkably similar to correct code." (footnote cites Bainbridge, 'Ironies of automation')

DORA 2025, Strong version control practices, pp. 55-56: "With a high degree of certainty, we found that AI adoption's positive benefits depend on respondents' frequency of version control commits." and "We have hypothesized that this is likely, in part, because it is harder to review larger batches of code."
DORA 2025, p. 56: "A key aspect of mature version control is its function as a \"psychological safety net.\""

DORA 2025, leadership guidance chapter: "Are teams incentivized to delegate tasks, verify AI output at scale, and share knowledge in new ways?" and "Rewarding behaviors like verification, delegation, prompt curation, and agent orchestration sends the right signals about what success looks like in an AI-accelerated environment." and "As developers delegate more work to AI tools, tasks like verification, orchestration, and workflow design become more central."
date_and_recency: Stack Overflow: fielded 29 May to 23 June 2025; results and launch post published 29 July 2025 (date in URL; page now shows re-publication date 29 December 2025). DORA: survey conducted 13 June to 21 July 2025, plus 78 in-depth interviews and 100+ hours of qualitative data; report v. 2025.2; publication around September 2025 [uncertain]. Both capture the mid-2025 tool generation, when agent use was still a minority (Stack Overflow: 37.9% of respondents 'No, and I don't plan to' use agents; 14.1% use them daily).
key_claims: Stack Overflow: adoption keeps rising (80% use AI tools in their workflow per the blog) while trust falls; more developers distrust AI accuracy (46%) than trust it (33%); the most common frustration is output that is 'almost right, but not quite', which feeds into time-consuming debugging; experienced developers are the most distrustful, which the authors read as 'a widespread need for human verification for those in roles with accountability'; when people don't trust AI's answers they turn to other people. DORA: AI is 'an amplifier' of existing organisational strengths and dysfunctions; 90% use AI at work, but 30% report little or no trust in AI-generated code, 'indicating a need for critical validation skills'; training should teach teams to 'critically guide, evaluate, and validate AI-generated work'; seven capabilities (AI stance, healthy data ecosystems, AI-accessible internal data, strong version control, small batches, user-centric focus, quality internal platforms) moderate AI's benefits; AI improves throughput but still increases delivery instability; individual friction shifts toward 'deciding and verifying'; verification, orchestration and workflow design become more central as work is delegated to AI.
headline_figures: Stack Overflow 2025, all respondents (31,476 responses to this question): 'AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite' 66%; 'Debugging AI-generated code is more time-consuming' 45.2%; 'I've become less confident in my own problem-solving' 20%; 'It's hard to understand how or why the code works' 16.3%; 'I haven't encountered any problems' 4%. Multi-select.

Stack Overflow 2025 trust in accuracy of AI output, all respondents (33,244 responses): highly trust 3.1%, somewhat trust 29.6%, somewhat distrust 26.1%, highly distrust 19.6% (page summarises as 46% distrust vs 33% trust). Remaining share not shown on the chart (likely neutral/unsure) [uncertain].

Stack Overflow 2025 trust, professional developers (25,701): highly trust 2.7%, somewhat trust 29.6%, somewhat distrust 26.3%, highly distrust 19.7%. Experienced devs, 10+ years (12,908): highly trust 2.5%, somewhat trust 28.6%, somewhat distrust 26.7%, highly distrust 20.7%. Learning to code (2,781): highly trust 6.1%, highly distrust 19.7%. (Summary text says 2.6% and 20% for experienced devs; chart shows 2.5% and 20.7%.)
Stack Overflow blog: trust in AI accuracy 'fallen from 40% in previous years to just 29% this year'; favourability down 'from 72% to 60% year over year'; 80% use AI tools in workflows.
Stack Overflow 2025 'would still ask a person' (29,163 responses): 'When I don't trust AI's answers' 75.3%; 'When I want to fully understand something' 61.3%.
Stack Overflow 2025 agents (31,877 responses): daily at work 14.1%, weekly 9%, monthly or infrequently 7.8%, 'No, and I don't plan to' 37.9%.
Stack Overflow 2025 complex tasks, professional developers: 'Bad' 22.8% plus 'Very poor' 18.6%; 'Very well' 3.9%.
DORA 2025: 90% of respondents use AI at work; more than 80% believe it increased productivity.
DORA 2025 trust in quality of AI-generated output (Figure 26): a great deal 4%, a lot 20%, somewhat 46%, a little 23%, not at all 7%. 70% some confidence; 30% 'little to no trust'.

DORA 2025 task chart: 56% of respondents whose jobs involve code review use AI for it; the chart also shows a second figure in parentheses (53%) whose meaning (likely share of all respondents) was not confirmed [uncertain].
DORA 2025 sample: 'nearly 5,000 technology professionals'; 15 candidate capabilities tested, seven retained.
sample_and_method: Stack Overflow: online survey, 49,009 usable responses from 177 countries (~15K excluded), mostly developers and people learning to code, recruited through Stack Overflow's own channels (onsite messaging, blog, newsletter, banners, social), so skewed toward engaged Stack Overflow users. Per-question response counts vary (AI questions roughly 29K-34K). Descriptive percentages only. DORA: global survey of nearly 5,000 technology professionals (software engineers and adjacent roles) run 13 June-21 July 2025, plus 78 in-depth interviews; latent-factor measures (AI adoption = use + reliance + trust), structural equation and Bayesian models reported with 89% credible intervals; capability effects are interactions (moderation) with AI adoption. Cross-sectional and self-reported.
what_is_measured: Neither source measures an interview format. Stack Overflow measures self-reported trust in AI output accuracy, frustrations with AI tools, agent use and when developers seek human help. DORA measures self-reported AI adoption, trust, and outcomes (individual effectiveness, throughput, instability, code quality, burnout, friction) and which organisational capabilities moderate AI's effects. Both bear on the construct 'judging and verifying AI output', which is a candidate thing for an interview to assess.
ai_policy_in_interview: Not applicable. (DORA's 'clear and communicated AI stance' is about workplace AI policy, not interviews.)
validity_evidence: None. Neither source reports criterion validity for any hiring method. DORA reports model fit and credible intervals for associations between capabilities, AI adoption and outcomes, not predictive validity of skills assessments.
relevance_to_angle: Supports 'working with an agent' as a thing to assess: the dominant failure mode developers report is output that is almost right (66%), so the scarce skill is spotting what is wrong in plausible code, not producing code. DORA says this directly: low trust indicates 'a need for critical validation skills', training should teach how to 'critically guide, evaluate, and validate AI-generated work', and individual work shifts to 'deciding and verifying' including 'assessing code that looks remarkably similar to correct code'. That is a ready-made case for interview tasks that hand a candidate agent output to review. Supports 'basic fluency' too: adoption is near universal (80-90%), so not using AI is unusual. The amplifier framing complicates a purely individual view: DORA says outcomes depend on systems (version control, small batches, platforms), so an interview that measures individual judgement captures only part of what makes AI pay off. Caution on wording: DORA's seven capabilities include strong version control practices but NOT code review; code review appears only as an AI use case (56%), a reason small batches matter ('harder to review larger batches of code') and in leadership guidance. Do not write that DORA names code review as a foundation.
limitations_stated: Stack Overflow methodology: respondents 'recruited primarily through channels owned by Stack Overflow', so 'highly-engaged' users are likely over-represented (statement truncated in extraction). DORA footnote 20: 'Although we try to do the work to create the conditions to speak causally, we don't want to give false assurances that we understand the underlying causal structure... ultimately, we're doing comparisons.' DORA footnote 19: 'given we have a snapshot, we're treating these highly co-determinant phenomena as unidimensional. If we had panel data, we could be more explicit about the cycle.' DORA, p. 50: 'we will continue validating, revising, and refining the DORA AI Capabilities Model with further research.' DORA p. 31 cautions 'against interpreting these findings of AI's ubiquity as an indication that all organizations should rapidly move to adopt AI'.
counter_evidence: The two surveys disagree on trust: DORA finds 70% have some confidence in AI output quality and 24% 'a great deal' or 'a lot', while Stack Overflow finds 46% distrust accuracy and only 3.1% highly trust. Question wording differs (quality vs accuracy; DORA has a 'somewhat' midpoint counted as confidence), so neither number should be quoted as 'developer trust' without its wording. DORA reads skepticism as healthy ('trust but verify' as 'a sign of mature adoption') and suggests developers 'may also already be accounting for this limitation', which cuts against framing distrust as a crisis. Stack Overflow's own blog swaps the 66%/45% figures, so secondary coverage citing '45% almost right' or '66% spend more time fixing' is wrong relative to the results page. Both are self-report from mid-2025, before wider agent use; agent use was a minority (31% use agents at work in any frequency). Neither shows that verification skill can be assessed in an interview or predicts job performance.
